newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia's Hun Sen dismisses U.S. stand on new PM.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's Hun Sen dismisses U.S. stand on new PM.

text.p: Cambodia's Second Prime Minister Hun Sen on Thursday dismissed a U.S. decision not to recognise his new co-premier, saying it was up to Cambodians to accept the appointment, not Americans.

Foreign Minister Ung Huot, a senior member of ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party, on Wednesday was chosen by the remnants of the royalist party to succeed Ranariddh.
Washington said there was no evidence that the party had elected him on a free and democratic basis.

"This is not so unusual," Hun Sen told a news conference, referring to the U.S. decision. "The most important thing for us is whether Ung Huot is acceptable to our people or not. We please our people, we can't please the Americans."
Hun Sen said he supported the royalist party's decision to nominate Ung Huot. He also said that steps were being taken to allay people's fears about human rights.
Hun Sen said Cambodia's King Norodom Sihanouk should return to the country from Beijing where he is undergoing medical treatment.
"It is in the interests of the Cambodian people and the international community that the king has better health and returns to Cambodia," he said. "The role of the king is very important."
Hun Sen ousted Ranariddh, Sihanouk's son, in a bloody coup in July 6. Western officials say up to 40 Cambodians have been killed since then, some of them after being tortured.
The United States said on Wednesday it was "very concerned" by the decision to make Ung Huot the country's co-prime minister and did not recognise him in that position.

"We are very concerned about the decision this morning to make the Cambodian foreign minister co-prime minister with Hun Sen," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told a news briefing in Washington.

"We urge the authorities in Phnom Penh to refrain from announcing a new first prime minister until Prince Ranariddh's political party has an opportunity to make a reasoned decision on this matter, free of coercion, free of intimidation," he said.
Ung Huot should not accept the job without Ranariddh expressing an opinion, he added.

The United States suspended aid to Cambodia for 30 days after Ranariddh's ouster and the U.S. Senate voted 99-0 late on Wednesday to halt U.S. aid until the secretary of state certified that the Cambodian government was established by free and fair elections, and not by force or coup.

Hun Sen said he still wanted the coalition between his Cambodian People's Party (CPP) and FUNCINPEC to remain in place and for elections to go ahead. He said he would abide by the 1991 Paris peace accord that officially ended Cambodia's war.
Ung Huot's nomination will be forwarded to the National Assembly when it opens on July 28.
Burns also said the United States was "very deeply troubled" by reports of killings in the aftermath of Hun Sen's ouster of his co-premier.
Ung Huot said earlier that Hun Sen was taking measures to end human rights abuses.
"When there is trouble, when there is fighting, we have to expect all this...but Cambodia should not go through this again," Ung Huot said.
"Hun Sen is taking measures to solve this by sending members of parliament from FUNCINPEC and the CPP to places where there is trouble. Measures are being taken every hour," he said.
Hun Sen confirmed the plan, saying: "This measure is aimed at putting an end to fear and intimidation."
Sihanouk, who on Thursday was meeting envoys from the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) in Beijing to discuss the crisis, has condemned the abuse of human rights since his son's ouster.
Ranariddh has since been travelling between Europe and the United States lobbying for support.

FUNCINPEC narrowly won a 1993 election supervised by the United Nations but agreed to a coalition with Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party (CPP) after Hun Sen objected to the poll result and the country faced splitting up along factional lines.
